facts.text: HADEP was a political party established on 11 May 1994 and dissolved on 13 March 2003, with Mr Ahmet Turan Demir as its general secretary elected in February 2003.

anchor.surface_text: 5.  HADEP was a political party which had been established on 11 May 1994. At the time of its dissolution on 13 March 2003 its general secretary was the second applicant, Mr Ahmet Turan Demir, who had been elected to that post in February 2003.

facts.text: In the general elections of 1995 and 1999, HADEP received 4.17% and 1,482,196 votes respectively but failed to pass the 10% threshold to enter the Turkish Parliament.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  In the general election held on 24 December 1995 HADEP received 1,171,623 votes, which represented 4.17% of the total number of votes cast. In the general election held on 18 April 1999 HADEP received 1,482,196 votes. However, as HADEP did not succeed in passing the required threshold of 10%, it was unable to be represented in the Grand National Assembly of Turkey following these two general elections

facts.text: During a National Security Council meeting on 18 December 1996, a decision was taken to dissolve HADEP, followed by raids on its branches and physical pressure on its administrators.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  The applicants submitted that, during a National Security Council (Milli Güvenlik Kurulu) meeting held on 18 December 1996, a decision had been taken to dissolve HADEP. In support of this assertion the applicants submitted to the Court a report which, they claimed, had been adopted by the National Security Council and which had subsequently been leaked to the press. The report, which is classified 'Secret', details a number of recommendations including “the control and pursuit of HADEP by the State in order to quell its activities”. Following this decision HADEP branches had been raided and its administrators had been subjected to physical pressure.

facts.text: Criminal proceedings were brought against several HADEP members for offences including spreading separatist propaganda and incitement to racial hatred, with some convicted and others acquitted or had sentences stayed.

anchor.surface_text: 8. On various dates criminal proceedings were brought against a number of members of HADEP who were holding executive positions within the party. Some of the proceedings were suspended while some ended in convictions. Some of them were convicted of spreading “separatist propaganda”, in breach of section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act, while others were convicted of “incitement to racial hatred and hostility in society on the basis of a distinction between social classes, races or religions”, in breach of Article 312 of the Criminal Code. A number of others were convicted of lending assistance to the PKK[1] in breach of Article 169 of the Criminal Code, for making speeches, allowing hunger strikers to use HADEP premises and for possessing a number of documents prepared by PKK members in a law-firm owned by one of them[2]. Some served their prison sentences while execution of the sentences of a number of others was stayed.

facts.text: On 29 January 1999, the chief prosecutor at the Court of Cassation brought proceedings before the Constitutional Court demanding HADEP's dissolution, alleging it was a centre of illegal activities against Turkey's integrity.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 29 January 1999 the chief prosecutor at the Court of Cassation brought proceedings before the Constitutional Court and demanded that HADEP be dissolved. The chief prosecutor argued that HADEP had become a “centre of illegal activities against the integrity of Turkey”. In support of his allegations the chief prosecutor referred to the criminal proceedings pending against members of HADEP and a number of activities of its members.

facts.text: On 25 February 1999, the chief prosecutor requested an interim ban on HADEP from the April elections, which the Constitutional Court refused on 8 March 1999.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  On 25 February 1999 the chief prosecutor asked the Constitutional Court to render an interim decision banning HADEP from taking part in the forthcoming April general and local elections. The chief prosecutor's request was refused by the Constitutional Court on 8 March 1999.

facts.text: On 5 April 1999, HADEP lawyers submitted a written defence to the Constitutional Court, alleging the dissolution request was based on the National Security Council decision and citing Convention rights violations.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 5 April 1999 lawyers for HADEP submitted a written defence to the Constitutional Court. They alleged that the chief prosecutor's request for the dissolution of HADEP had been made as a result of the National Security Council's above-mentioned decision (see paragraph 7). They further argued, inter alia, that as it was not clear what the accusations against HADEP were, it was not possible for them to make full use of their defence rights. The lawyers relied on Articles 6, 9, 10, 11 and 14 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, and asked the Constitutional Court to take into account the decisions and judgments of the European Court of Human Rights in cases concerning the dissolution of a number of other political parties in Turkey.

facts.text: On 13 March 2003, the Constitutional Court unanimously decided to dissolve HADEP, finding it a centre of illegal activities aiding the PKK, based on Articles 68 and 69 of the Constitution and sections 101 and 103 of the Political Parties Act.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  In its decision of 13 March 2003 the Constitutional Court decided unanimously to dissolve HADEP. The Constitutional Court based its decision on Articles 68 and 69 of the Constitution and sections 101 and 103 of the Political Parties Act (Law no. 2820). In arriving at its conclusion, the Constitutional Court took account of the activities of certain leaders and members of HADEP and concluded that HADEP had become a centre of illegal activities which included aiding and abetting the PKK.

facts.text: During HADEP's 1996 annual general meeting, a non-member took down the Turkish flag and replaced it with a PKK flag and a poster of Abdullah Öcalan; HADEP's general secretary did not stop this.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  The Constitutional Court noted, in particular, that during HADEP's annual general meeting in 1996 a non-HADEP member wearing a mask had taken down the Turkish flag and replaced it with a PKK flag and a poster of the then leader of the PKK, Abdullah Öcalan. During the same meeting slogans had also been chanted in support of the PKK and its leader[3]. The then general secretary of HADEP Mr Murat Bozlak, who was present during the meeting on that day, had done nothing to stop the Turkish flag being taken down and had stated during his speech that “the existence of the Kurds in Turkey, who were not allowed to speak their mother tongue, had been denied.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court banned 46 HADEP members from political party activities for five years and ordered HADEP's property transferred to the Treasury.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  As an ancillary measure under Article 69 § 9 of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court banned 46 HADEP members and leaders from becoming founder members, ordinary members, leaders or auditors of any other political party for a period of five years[5]. The Constitutional Court also ordered the transfer of HADEP's property to the Treasury.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court's decision to dissolve HADEP became final upon its publication in the Official Gazette on 19 July 2003.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  The decision of the Constitutional Court became final following its publication in the Official Gazette on 19 July 2003.

facts.text: The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 September 2003, alleging that HADEP's dissolution violated Article 11 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 1.  The case originated in an application (no. 28003/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish political party Halkın Demokrasi Partisi (People's Democracy Party, hereinafter referred to as “HADEP”) and a Turkish national, Mr Ahmet Turan Demir (“the applicants”), on 1 September 2003.

facts.text: Mr Ahmet Turan Demir was elected HADEP's general secretary in February 2003, before the party's dissolution on 13 March 2003.

anchor.surface_text: At the time of its dissolution on 13 March 2003 its general secretary was the second applicant, Mr Ahmet Turan Demir, who had been elected to that post in February 2003.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court found that HADEP had become a centre of illegal activities including aiding and abetting the PKK, based on members' speeches, activities, and possession of PKK propaganda materials.

anchor.surface_text: The Constitutional Court considered the taking down of the Turkish flag as proof of the links between HADEP and the PKK. It further considered that the references made by Mr Bozlak to Turkey's fight against terrorism as an “occupation” and portraying Kurds as a separate nation showed that Mr Bozlak was supporting the PKK[4]. ... Activities by members of the People's Democracy Party and the evidence [in our possession] clearly show the links between the respondent party and the PKK. The following incidents and activities – and many others and judgments rendered by courts – are proof of the connection and support between the People's Democracy Party and the PKK terrorist organisation: ...

facts.text: HADEP had branches in 47 cities and hundreds of districts, controlled 37 municipalities after 1999 local elections, and joined the Socialist International in 2002.

anchor.surface_text: In local elections held on 18 April 1999 HADEP won control of 37 municipalities. It had branches in 47 cities and in hundreds of districts. In 2002 HADEP became a member of the Socialist International.

facts.text: The chief prosecutor alleged HADEP had close ties with the PKK and was controlled by it, citing the 1996 incident where the Turkish flag was replaced by a PKK flag at HADEP's annual meeting.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  The chief prosecutor maintained in his written submissions of 9 April 1999 that HADEP had close ties with the PKK, and alleged that the former was being controlled by the latter. The chief prosecutor also repeated his request for HADEP to be dissolved before the elections which were to be held on 18 April 1999.

facts.text: HADEP representatives told the Constitutional Court that the person who took down the Turkish flag was not a party member and that HADEP condemned the incident publicly.

anchor.surface_text: 13. During the proceedings, in their submissions to the Constitutional Court HADEP's representatives drew attention to the fact that the person who had taken down the flag was not a member of the party. They further stated that, immediately after the incident the HADEP congress had publicly condemned the incident.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court referred to Article 11 and Article 17 of the Convention, concluding that a political party supporting terrorism cannot be allowed to continue to exist.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  The Constitutional Court referred to Article 11 of the Convention in its judgment and stated that the rights guaranteed in that provision were not absolute and could be restricted in the circumstances listed in Article 11 § 2 of the Convention. It also referred to Article 17 of the Convention, and reached the following conclusion: “Carrying out activities, by relying on democratic rights and freedoms, against the indivisible unity of the State with its nation is unacceptable. In such circumstances it is the duty and raison d'être of the State to prevent the abuse of these rights and freedoms. Allowing a political party which supports terrorism and which is supported by terrorism to continue to exist cannot be contemplated.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court banned 46 HADEP members from political party activities for five years and ordered HADEP's property transferred to the Treasury.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  As an ancillary measure under Article 69 § 9 of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court banned 46 HADEP members and leaders from becoming founder members, ordinary members, leaders or auditors of any other political party for a period of five years[5]. The Constitutional Court also ordered the transfer of HADEP's property to the Treasury.

facts.text: The Constitutional Court's decision was published in the Official Gazette on 19 July 2003, making it final.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that HADEP had effectively been dissolved by the decision adopted by the National Security Council on 18 December 1996 and that the subsequent proceedings before the Constitutional Court had merely been attempts to legalise that dissolution.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants alleged, in particular, that the dissolution of HADEP by the Constitutional Court had been in breach of Article 11 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the interference was “prescribed by law” as the measures ordered by the Constitutional Court were based on Articles 68 and 69 of the Constitution, as well as sections 101 and 103 of the Political Parties Act (Law no. 2820).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court observed the dissolution was based on the cited legal provisions and thus prescribed by law.

arguments.claim: The applicants denied that they had ever been a threat to Turkish society and argued that the dissolution of HADEP had thus been devoid of any legitimate aim.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants denied that they had ever been a threat to Turkish society and argued that the dissolution of HADEP had thus been devoid of any legitimate aim.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court hesitated whether maintaining indivisible unity pursued legitimate aims but considered it related to necessity.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the dissolution of HADEP had pursued the legitimate aims of preventing disorder, protecting the rights of others and protecting territorial integrity and thus preserving national security.

anchor.surface_text: The Government maintained that the dissolution of HADEP had pursued the legitimate aims of preventing disorder, protecting the rights of others and protecting territorial integrity and thus preserving national security.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court hesitated whether maintaining indivisible unity pursued legitimate aims but considered it related to necessity.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that dissolving a political party did not comply with the needs of a democratic society and made it impossible to achieve pluralism; the dissolution of HADEP was not necessary in a democratic society.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants argued that dissolving a political party did not comply with the needs of a democratic society and made it impossible to achieve pluralism. The dissolution of HADEP was not necessary in a democratic society.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the dissolution was not necessary in a democratic society and thus disproportionate.

arguments.claim: The applicants submitted that HADEP had never done anything to damage the indivisible unity of Turkey or harboured that aim but sought democratic rights for citizens of Kurdish origin.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants further submitted that, contrary to what was suggested by the Government, HADEP had never done anything to damage the indivisible unity of Turkey or harboured that aim. What it had sought to achieve in particular was to ensure that citizens of Kurdish origin had the rights to be educated in their mother tongue, to listen to radio and watch television programmes in the Kurdish language, to sustain their culture and to exercise their democratic right to participate in the political arena.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered HADEP's aims democratic and peaceful and found no sufficient evidence of support for terrorism.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that the Constitutional Court had based its decision on speeches and activities of some HADEP members, some acquitted, and some activities/statements were by non-members.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants maintained that the Constitutional Court had based its decision on a number of speeches and activities that had allegedly been made or carried out by members of HADEP. They pointed out that in respect of some of these speeches and activities a number of HADEP members had been tried but acquitted. Nevertheless, this had not prevented the Constitutional Court from relying on them in dissolving HADEP. Moreover, some of the activities and statements relied on by the Constitutional Court had been those of persons who were not members of HADEP.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the Constitutional Court relied on these allegations despite acquittals and non-members' actions, but found the threshold too low.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that most impugned activities and statements attributed to HADEP members remained within permissible limits of freedom of speech and association.

anchor.surface_text: Finally, the applicants argued that most of the impugned activities and statements which the Constitutional Court attributed to HADEP members had remained within the permissible limits of the freedom of speech and association.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held that sharp criticisms did not incite violence and were protected speech under Articles 10 and 11.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that no political party should be allowed to participate in activities aimed at destroying the unity and integrity of a State or disturbing national solidarity.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that no political party should be allowed to participate in activities whose aim was to destroy the unity and integrity of a State or to disturb national solidarity.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court acknowledged the legitimate aim of protecting national unity and security but scrutinized necessity and proportionality.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that HADEP and its members were representatives of the terrorist organisation PKK and their activities could not be regarded as protected freedom of assembly and association.

anchor.surface_text: The actions of members of HADEP, as well as the activities of HADEP as a political party, which were set out in the decision of the Constitutional Court, revealed a connection between HADEP and the PKK. It was thus accepted that both HADEP and its members were representatives of the terrorist organisation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court did not find sufficient evidence that HADEP had associated with or encouraged PKK terrorism.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the present case differed from previous political party dissolution cases as HADEP was dissolved based on members' activities, showing it aimed to divide the country by applauding PKK terrorist acts.

anchor.surface_text: In the Government's opinion the present application differed from the previous cases concerning the dissolution of political parties in Turkey which had been examined by the Court. Those political parties had been dissolved on the basis of their party programmes. HADEP, on the other hand, had been dissolved on the basis of activities carried out by its members. Such activities showed that HADEP had not been bound by the rules of democratic debate, but had instead tended towards the aim of dividing the country by applauding the terrorist acts perpetrated by the PKK.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the dissolution was based on insufficient evidence and the threshold was too low.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the PKK was a terrorist organisation condemned by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe and the European Union.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the PKK was a terrorist organisation. In this connection they referred, inter alia, to the “strong condemnation” by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe in its recommendation no. 1377 of 25 June 1998 of “the violence and terrorism perpetrated by the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has contributed to population displacement and movements”. They also pointed to the fact that the PKK was regarded as a terrorist organisation by the European Union (see 2002/976/CFSP; Council Common Position of 12 December 2002 updating Common Position 2001/931/CFSP on the application of specific measures to combat terrorism and repealing Common Position 2002/340/CFSP).

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that HADEP bore some responsibility for terrorism problems in Turkey and its dissolution was not disproportionate.

anchor.surface_text: Regard being had to the difficulties in fighting terrorism, it was justified on the basis of the evidence relied on by the Constitutional Court that HADEP bore some responsibility for the problems caused by terrorism in Turkey. Thus, HADEP's dissolution had not been a disproportionate measure and it had not amounted to a violation of Article 11 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the dissolution disproportionate and not necessary in a democratic society.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that a political party may campaign for change only if means are legal and democratic and the change is compatible with democratic principles.

anchor.surface_text: In support of their arguments the Government referred to the Court's case-law and submitted that a political party could promote a change in the law or the legal and constitutional structures of the State on two conditions: firstly, the means used to that end had to be legal and democratic; secondly, the change proposed had itself to be compatible with fundamental democratic principles.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court agreed that parties inciting violence or opposing democracy cannot claim Convention protection.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that the decision of the National Security Council had influenced the judges of the Constitutional Court and that there was systematic pressure on the Court damaging its independence and impartiality, contrary to Article 6.

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the applicants argued that the decision of the National Security Council had influenced the judges of the Constitutional Court in reaching their decision to dissolve HADEP.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found Article 6 not applicable to political party dissolution proceedings as political rights are at issue.

arguments.claim: The applicants complained that the Constitutional Court had not ensured that they and their witnesses could attend the proceedings and had failed to hold a hearing, violating Article 6.

anchor.surface_text: Under Article 6 § 3 (b) and (d) of the Convention the applicants complained that the Constitutional Court had not ensured that they and their witnesses could attend the proceedings and had failed to hold a hearing.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held Article 6 was not applicable ratione materiae to these proceedings.

arguments.claim: The applicants complained that the dissolution of HADEP violated their rights under Articles 9 and 10 and that HADEP was dissolved because it was regarded as a Kurdish party, violating Article 14.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants complained that the dissolution of HADEP had violated their rights guaranteed by Articles 9 and 10 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered these complaints related to Article 11 and did not examine separately.

arguments.claim: The applicants complained that the transfer of HADEP's possessions to the Treasury violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and that dissolution prevented HADEP from representing its voters, violating Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants also complained that the transfer of HADEP's possessions to the Treasury had been in violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Finally, the applicants alleged a breach of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 in that HADEP's dissolution had prevented it from representing its millions of voters.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found these complaints secondary effects of dissolution and did not examine separately.

arguments.claim: The Court must review under Article 11 the decisions of national authorities exercising their discretion, ensuring proportionality and relevant and sufficient reasons.

anchor.surface_text: When the Court carries out its scrutiny, its task is not to substitute its own view for that of the relevant national authorities but rather to review under Article 11 of the Convention the decisions they delivered in the exercise of their discretion.

arguments.claim: The exceptions in Article 11 are to be construed strictly; only convincing and compelling reasons can justify restrictions on political parties' freedom of association.

anchor.surface_text: Furthermore, the exceptions set out in Article 11 of the Convention are, where political parties are concerned, to be construed strictly; only convincing and compelling reasons can justify restrictions on such parties' freedom of association.

arguments.claim: Contracting States have only a limited margin of appreciation in Article 11 cases, subject to rigorous European supervision including law and decisions by independent courts.

anchor.surface_text: In determining whether a necessity within the meaning of Article 11 § 2 of the Convention exists, the Contracting States have only a limited margin of appreciation, which goes hand in hand with rigorous European supervision embracing both the law and the decisions applying it, including those given by independent courts.

arguments.claim: A political party may campaign for change only if means are legal and democratic and the change is compatible with fundamental democratic principles.

anchor.surface_text: a political party may campaign for a change in the law or the legal and constitutional structures of the State on two conditions: firstly, the means used to that end must in every respect be legal and democratic, and secondly, the change proposed must itself be compatible with fundamental democratic principles.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the dissolution of HADEP was a drastic measure and was not necessary in a democratic society, thus breaching Article 11.

anchor.surface_text: Accordingly, the Court finds that the dissolution of HADEP breached Article 11 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded the dissolution was disproportionate and unnecessary in a democratic society.

holdings.text: The Court finds that the second applicant Mr Ahmet Demir was the general secretary of HADEP at the time of its dissolution and can thus claim to be a victim within the meaning of Article 34 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Court observes that the second applicant Mr Ahmet Demir was elected as HADEP's general secretary in February 2003, that is before the Constitutional Court decided to dissolve HADEP on 13 March 2003 and thus while HADEP continued to exist as a political party.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court held that Mr Demir's election before dissolution and lack of ban imposed does not negate victim status under Article 34.

holdings.text: The Court takes the view that HADEP's dissolution and the measures which accompanied it amounted to an interference with the applicants' exercise of their right to freedom of association under Article 11.

anchor.surface_text: The parties accepted that HADEP's dissolution and the measures which accompanied it amounted to an interference with the applicants' exercise of their right to freedom of association. The Court takes the same view.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court agreed with parties that dissolution constituted interference with Article 11 rights.

holdings.text: The Court observes that the dissolution was based on Articles 68 and 69 of the Constitution and sections 101 and 103 of the Political Parties Act and was thus prescribed by law within the meaning of Article 11 § 2.

anchor.surface_text: The Court observes that the dissolution was based on the above-mentioned Articles of the Constitution and the Political Parties Act and was thus prescribed by law.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the legal basis for dissolution satisfied the 'prescribed by law' requirement.

holdings.text: The Court hesitates whether the dissolution pursued the legitimate aims of preventing disorder, protecting the rights of others and protecting territorial integrity but considers this question closely related to necessity of the interference.

anchor.surface_text: The Court observes that the Constitutional Court decided to dissolve HADEP because it was deemed to be a centre of illegal activities against the indivisible unity of the State with its nation (see paragraph 16 above). Contrary to what was submitted by the Government, however, the Court has hesitations as to whether the dissolution of a political party in order to maintain the indivisible unity of the State with its nation can be said to have pursued the legitimate aims of preventing disorder, protecting the rights of others and protecting territorial integrity and thus preserving national security.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court was uncertain if maintaining indivisible unity qualified as a legitimate aim but linked this to necessity analysis.

holdings.text: The Court finds that the dissolution of HADEP was not necessary in a democratic society and thus was disproportionate, breaching Article 11 of the Convention.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court concluded the dissolution was a drastic measure not justified by a pressing social need and disproportionate to the aims pursued.

holdings.text: The Court finds that the Constitutional Court's decision to dissolve HADEP was not based on an acceptable assessment of the relevant facts.

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes the Constitutional Court relied on these allegations despite acquittals and non-members' actions, but found the threshold too low.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the Constitutional Court relied on insufficient evidence including acts by non-members and acquitted members, lowering the threshold improperly.

holdings.text: The Court holds that Article 6 of the Convention is not applicable ratione materiae to the proceedings concerning the dissolution of HADEP and thus declares the complaint under Article 6 inadmissible.

anchor.surface_text: It sees no reason to come to a different conclusion and concludes that Article 6 of the Convention is not applicable in the instant case. It follows that this part of the application is incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 of the Convention, and must be rejected in accordance with Article 35 § 4 of the Convention.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court held that political party dissolution concerns political rights and thus Article 6 procedural guarantees do not apply.

holdings.text: The Court holds that there is no need to examine separately the complaints under Articles 9, 10 and 14 of the Convention or the complaints under Articles 1 and 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: However, since they relate to the same matters as those considered above under Article 11 of the Convention, the Court does not consider it necessary to examine them separately.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court considered these complaints closely related to Article 11 and thus did not examine them separately.

holdings.text: The Court holds that the second applicant Mr Ahmet Turan Demir is to be paid EUR 24,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage and the applicants jointly EUR 2,200 for costs and expenses, with default interest.

holdings.text: The Court dismisses the remainder of the applicants' claim for just satisfaction, including pecuniary damage claims.
